topics.topic: First-release delivery, versioning, and enforcement of agent instructions
questions: Before the second-release manifest description exists, who supplies the rule to the agent, through what concrete input or trust boundary, how is its version tied to the running Registry contract, and what happens when that instruction is absent or stale?

During the first release, who turns the governance rule into instructions the agent actually receives, through what system or trust boundary, at what point in a session or run, and what observable failure occurs if those instructions are absent or stale?

quotes:
As in R0-68 and R0-90, this is a rule on the writer — the owner, and the agent
through Kernel — not a check of Registry: Registry cannot tell what a word
means, refuses no name for its content and searches no text for words; a
name that breaks the rule does reach the agent. The owner learns the rule
from the governance; the owner interface does not show it. The agent learns
it from the description of the room name and the alias in Registry's
manifest record (R0-78). That description is changed in the second release
(R0-100); until then the rule binds the owner, and the agent through the
governance's instructions to it.

The **first release** is the release assembled from this specification as it
stands with R0-99 (State 8) and admitted by the Code Factory (Stage 9).
Registry goes into production with it, and with it makes the one import
(R0-79, R0-98).

In Registry's derived manifest record (R0-78), adding a room, publishing a
pointer and withdrawing one are `state-transition`. Each such write of the
agent waits for the owner's approval of its exact request, unless the owner
gave that flow version a standing approval for the node (K-08). A request for
access stays `draft-write`: it changes no access, replaces the session's
earlier request (R0-47) and is itself a question to the owner.

judgement.divergence: One implementation injects a current, versioned governance instruction into every first-release agent run and blocks the write when it is absent or stale; another performs no delivery or runtime check and Registry accepts the prohibited name, which the owner, later agents and the external AI provider notice.
judgement.why: The first-release text promises that governance instructions bind the agent but names neither the actor or trust boundary that delivers them nor an observable failure for missing or stale instructions, allowing the same admissible write to produce different visible names.

events: Cabinet Kernel starts a run for the agent on the granted project.
The agent prepares an add-room request naming the room "Bathroom for wheelchair".
The owner approves the exact request and Cabinet Kernel submits it to Registry.
Registry applies its stated name checks and returns the resulting room.
outcomes: An implementation supplies the current governance instruction to the run, so the agent uses a neutral room name.
An implementation supplies no instruction or a stale one, so Registry accepts the prohibited name and later returns it to agents.

topics.topic: Owner delivery and acknowledgement of room-name and alias rules
questions: What concrete governance artifact or action teaches the owner this rule, when must that happen, and what prevents an owner who has not received or acknowledged it from writing a prohibited name?
What concrete action ensures that the owner receives and acknowledges the room-name and alias rule before writing either value, and what happens if that action has not occurred?

quotes:
A room is named by its purpose and, where needed, its number or position —
"Bathroom 1", "Kitchen", "Bedroom with balcony" — never by a person, nor by a
person's condition, health, disability, age or other need. What the work
does for such a need — an adapted shower, a ramp — is the content of the
work and lives in the documents of the service that owns them, PresuPro's
estimate among them, never in a room name. The alias (R0-82) follows the
same rule.

As in R0-68 and R0-90, this is a rule on the writer — the owner, and the agent
through Kernel — not a check of Registry: Registry cannot tell what a word
means, refuses no name for its content and searches no text for words; a
name that breaks the rule does reach the agent. The owner learns the rule
from the governance; the owner interface does not show it. The agent learns
it from the description of the room name and the alias in Registry's
manifest record (R0-78). That description is changed in the second release
(R0-100); until then the rule binds the owner, and the agent through the
governance's instructions to it.

Like room names (R0-68), the alias is a rule on its writer, the owner: Registry
does not inspect it, and an alias that breaks the rule is not refused. A
project without an alias is shown to the agent by its id. Projects imported
under a person's name (R0-79) are renamed by the owner after the import.

topics.topic: Adding-room idempotency replay, conflict, retention, and scope
questions: What is the replay behaviour recorded in the manifest for adding a room: what does Registry return for the same key and equal input, what happens if the same key is reused with different input, and for how long and within what scope is the key remembered?

quotes:
2. Registry keeps the request id with the record the create made, written once
   (M01, M03, M04, M05).

4. A request id is looked up among the records of the same model — for 'add a
   room' and 'publish an artifact pointer', only those of the project the
   call names, so a record of another project is never reached through it.
   A create whose request id such a record carries is
   a repeat when the facts it supplies equal that record's current facts of
   the same kind: Registry answers the record as it stands now and changes
   nothing. A publish's repeat answers the pointer whatever its status now; it
   neither supersedes nor makes a version (R0-17, R0-88).

5. A create whose request id an existing record carries, with facts that
   differ from that record's current ones — a different value, or the record
   corrected since — is refused, and nothing changes; the caller reads the
   record.

8. A request id leaves its record with the values anonymisation or erasure
   removes (M01, M04); a create arriving after that with the same request id
   is a new create, checked as any create — a customer it names that is now
   restricted, ended or erased refuses it — and, when accepted, answered with
   the new record it made, so it is not silent (R0-36, owner, 2026-11-01).
judgement.why: State 2 A01 specifies that room request ids are scoped to the named project, retained with the room record, return the room as it currently stands for an equal replay, and refuse different facts without changing anything.

author_guidance: Before editing, identify the decision's owning state from the phase purpose, question_scope and layer obligations, then choose a disposition for each topic that awaits one.
fixed: repair a decision the owning state must make; do not add later-layer implementation choices merely to close a topic. Record the fix commit and review the changed text once.

carried: name the receiving layer and use --what to preserve the choice, its options and consequences, and the required guarantee every option must keep. Decide any guarantee owned here before carrying its execution onward.
accepted: explain why the remaining choice is permitted. Bring an unresolved product choice to the owner with its options and consequences; absence of a quoted requirement does not decide it.
contradiction and standard_violation take no disposition: repair the offending text in its owning state and review the change. Deterministic transition findings must also close through their checks.
